deep_why: This attack reconstructs private training text by exploiting how frozen neural models leak information through attention patterns. The core principle is that even when model weights don't change, the way the model focuses on different parts of its input creates measurable signals about what text was present. By examining which positions the frozen layers attend to, the attacker can infer which words were in the original message. The low-rank adapter update then reveals the text at fine-grain resolution through solving for what small changes best explain the observed attention shifts. This works because attention patterns compress information about input content into a readable form, and the problem structure forces a unique solution when you also enforce that the reconstructed text must read naturally. The practical threat is that privacy protections from freezing weights don't actually prevent leakage of the underlying training data.

Graph clustering aims to group similar nodes, but nodes have both structural patterns (who they connect to) and meaning patterns (what they represent). The method works by scoring pairs as similar or different twice: once based on graph connections, once based on semantic meaning. The insight is that each scoring independently identifies genuine patterns, and their agreement flags truly reliable examples while disagreement flags noise. By comparing nodes across both views, the system finds which comparisons are stable and trustworthy, rather than treating all edges equally. The curriculum principle ensures harder distinctions get learned first, building a robust foundation. This works because real clusters form at the intersection of these two independent signals, so consistency across both dimensions proves true affinity.

Recommending items requires combining multiple data sources: what users have clicked (behavior history), text descriptions, images, and item-to-item relationships. Each source tells a different story about an item. The core principle is alignment: if the behavior-based view and the description-based view represent the same item differently, one or both must be wrong, so the system learns by maximizing their mutual agreement. The method separately extracts patterns from each view, then iteratively tunes them so predictions stay consistent across all views. This works because true semantic meaning must appear across all modalities—text, image, and user behavior should point toward the same real properties. By forcing agreement, the system filters out view-specific noise and keeps only robust shared meaning.

Emotional support requires both logic and empathy, which pull in different directions. The method integrates explicit symbolic reasoning (rule-based inference about problems) with learned neural understanding (sensing emotional tone). The core soundness comes from the principle that true solutions must satisfy both: they must be logically coherent AND emotionally appropriate. By combining interpretable rules that can be traced and verified with learned patterns that capture subtle emotional nuance, the system produces responses that a user can understand and trust. This hybrid approach works because emotions and logic are not antagonistic—good support actually requires both simultaneously, and maintaining both through separate, then coordinated pathways ensures neither gets abandoned.

Answering questions about personal data requires understanding both what events occurred in someone's life and when they occurred. Many real questions need aggregation over time (counting workouts in a month) or filtering by temporal rules (spending in Q3). The benchmark's power comes from mixing analytic requirements with temporal constraints, creating questions that force systems to correctly parse time expressions and combine multiple conditions. This works because time is often ignored in text systems, and temporal understanding is mathematically independent from semantic understanding—a system cannot succeed by accident through shortcuts. Benchmarks with realistic temporal structure reveal whether systems genuinely solve the reasoning problem or simply pattern-match.

Education systems must predict what students know based on which problems they got right or wrong. Existing methods represent students and problems with learned numbers. The soundness of adding language model help is that language captures semantic relationships: a reading-comprehension problem and a vocabulary problem both test language understanding, so text representations reveal their shared conceptual roots. The method bridges the gap by aligning the number-based representations (which are optimized for predicting right/wrong) with text-based representations (which encode semantic meaning), ensuring the combined system uses the full context. This works because numbers and text see different aspects of the same problem—numbers see the prediction targets, text sees the conceptual structure. Alignment fuses both perspectives into more complete understanding.

Classifying images requires recognizing both visual patterns and semantic meaning. The core challenge is that models trained on limited image classes learn shortcuts that fail on new classes or when image distributions shift. The method works by extracting external knowledge (facts about each image from language models) and using dual teachers to teach the classifier: one teacher scores the classifier's confidence, the other confirms whether the prediction is actually reliable. By explicitly comparing how different teachers rank the same image, the system identifies and downweights unreliable predictions during training. This works because overfitting to training classes leaves the model confident on impossible examples—multiple independent raters catch this by disagreeing. Forcing agreement across diverse judges prevents shortcuts and builds genuine understanding.

Web browsers store login cookies to remember users across multiple visits. When sites set cookies to work across subdomains for convenience, a compromised subdomain can steal those cookies and use them to impersonate the user across all other subdomains. The vulnerability is structural: cookie scope assumes all subdomains are equally trusted, but security requires that one weak link breaks the chain. The attack works through subdomain takeover (compromising one subdomain) followed by cookie interception (reading all shared cookies). The principle exposed is that convenience defaults violate a fundamental security rule: trust boundaries should shrink, not expand, as you move to less controlled environments. This works because network-level sharing creates no cryptographic separation—if physical access allows reading one cookie, all cookies in that scope are visible.

Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions by fetching documents then having a model read them. The problem arises when different documents contradict each other, confusing the model into generating inconsistent answers. The core principle is conflict detection: by measuring how uncertain the model becomes when seeing different documents, the system identifies which documents create contradictions. These conflict signals then guide training in two ways: during supervised learning, hard conflicting examples become instructive training data; during preference learning, the model learns to favor consistent interpretations over contradictory ones. This works because contradictions create measurable uncertainty in model probabilities—the model's own confusion reveals which document pairs genuinely conflict, without needing external labels.

Log parsing extracts structured event types from unstructured text logs. Logs contain constant parts (fixed messages) and variable parts (data like IP addresses or error codes). Existing methods focus only on constants, treating variables as noise. The insight is that variables are predictive signals: if logs with the same error code behave similarly in production, then clustering by error codes improves grouping. The method works by grouping logs first by variable content, then asking language models to identify patterns only within each group. This drastically reduces the number of tokens shown to language models (since groups are pre-filtered) and increases accuracy (since language models see context-relevant examples). This works because variables encode causal information about what actually went wrong, not just how it was described—ignoring them discards genuine signal.

Detecting abnormal graphs in real data is hard because training data typically contains some hidden anomalies (unlabeled misbehavior) despite claims of being clean. The method works by modeling uncertainty: representing detection scores as ranges rather than single numbers. When a sample looks anomalous according to some detectors but normal according to others, the system treats it as uncertain, and during training, gradually reduces its influence on learning. This iterative process balances two goals: down-weight likely anomalies in training so they don't corrupt the model, but also learn to detect them. This works because mathematical certainty about abnormality can only come from seeing large numbers of confirmed examples, so expressing doubt about borderline cases prevents the model from learning false patterns from mislabeled data. The uncertainty framework makes learning robust to the inherent noise in real-world unlabeled datasets.

Text-attributed graphs combine network structure with text on nodes. The method uses language models to generate initial representations, then fine-tunes them to transfer across different datasets. The core principle is that general semantic understanding transfers (a graph about publications and a graph about citations both involve research) but structure differs per domain. The system learns a common representation through dual-view consistency: comparing the language model's output in-domain against cross-domain examples, which preserves semantic alignment while adapting to local structure. Then it applies dimensionality reduction that respects both the learned semantics and the network structure. This works because domain-general text understanding is reusable, but structure-specific patterns must be learned fresh—separating these concerns into aligned stages ensures neither dominates the other.

Knowledge graphs answer questions by finding relevant subgraphs, but single-perspective retrieval may miss complementary facts. The method models multiple viewpoints within a question: for a query like 'awards of female scientists', different intents could emphasize female identity, scientific fields, or award types. By extracting multiple topic-based viewpoints and letting each one propose subgraph candidates, the system captures diverse reasoning paths. The key principle is end-to-end optimization: measure which combinations of candidates actually improve the final answer quality, then train the topic selector and candidate scorer to prefer beneficial combinations. This works because some facts are individually irrelevant but collectively necessary—only by observing which groups of facts together produce correct answers can the system learn which combinations matter.

This workshop examines how data and technology serve cities by improving services and decision-making. The core principle is that data alone is inert—outcomes depend on how data is collected, processed, and applied. Different computational methods (machine learning, simulation, optimization) produce different insights from the same data, and different integration approaches (silo versus holistic) lead to different impacts on citizen experience. The workshop works because urban problems require interdisciplinary understanding: data scientists, engineers, policymakers, and residents all have valid perspectives on what constitutes improvement, and dialogue across these views prevents technology from optimizing for wrong targets.

Graph classification divides graphs into categories, but real data often has many rare classes (tail classes) with few examples. Standard approaches learn to recognize common classes well and bias predictions toward them, leaving rare classes misidentified. The method uses evidential reasoning: instead of a single score per class, it maintains a distribution of beliefs and measures uncertainty. Multiple expert classifiers each express their views with uncertainty, then these views combine through formal evidence theory. The core principle is that diversity reduces bias: when multiple independent experts disagree about tail-class examples, their disagreement is preserved as uncertainty rather than forced into a false consensus. This works because tail classes are genuinely harder to recognize with little data, and expressing that difficulty honestly prevents overconfident wrong predictions while directing training focus toward truly informative examples.
